design_detail: Systematic review and two-level multivariate mixed-effects meta-analysis (GLLAMM, Stata 13; MOOSE reporting) of cross-sectional comparisons of neurocognitive test scores between adolescents and young adults (sample mean age 26 or younger) with frequent, heavy or problematic cannabis use and comparison participants with minimal use. 69 samples (the Table's rows, from 62 publications, 1973-2017) and 384 Hedges-corrected standardized mean differences classified into 10 cognitive domains; longitudinal studies contributed baseline data only. Searches 10 December 2016 to 12 May 2017; English-language, peer-reviewed studies; no registered protocol. Predetermined moderators included age, age at first use and the abstinence required before testing.
can_establish: The average size and spread of reported cross-sectional differences in neurocognitive test scores between young people who use cannabis frequently and comparison groups up to May 2017, by cognitive domain, and whether those differences vary with study-level features such as the abstinence required before testing or treatment seeking.
cannot_establish: Whether cannabis causes the differences (no pre-use baseline; raw scores not adjusted for confounders); whether deficits recover in any person who stops (the abstinence result compares different studies, not the same people over time); effects of years of use into adulthood (longitudinal follow-ups and IQ-only studies were excluded); or the clinical meaning of a group difference for individuals.

sample.recruitment: Database search (PubMed, PsycINFO, Academic Search Premier, Scopus) run independently by two authors from 10 December 2016 to 12 May 2017, plus the bibliographies of four qualitative reviews; English-language, peer-reviewed studies from database inception (Methods › Search Strategies and Study Selection; Abstract › Data Sources). Seven investigators supplied supplementary data from their studies (Article information, Additional Contributions). Participants came from the included studies, 12 of them treatment-seeking samples; median group size 23 with cannabis and 30 comparison participants, and 31 of 69 cannabis groups had 20 or fewer people (editors' count from the Table).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human adolescents or young adults with a sample mean age of 26 or younger; heavy, frequent or problematic cannabis use as the primary variable; cannabis not identified solely as a comorbidity of another substance use or mental disorder; not focused on acute effects; an appropriate comparison group; at least one standardized neurocognitive test; written in English; data sufficient for an effect size. Only cross-sectional data (baseline data from longitudinal studies). Full texts excluded (Figure 1): 67 no relevant neurocognitive testing, 48 no cannabis-only group, 35 outside the age range, 34 no appropriate comparison group, 29 measures only during neuroimaging, 19 reviews, 17 insufficient data, 16 participants with psychosis, 8 acute use, 7 prenatal exposure, 5 insufficient cannabis data, 3 IQ measures only, 1 intervention study; 5 articles removed for overlapping samples (Methods › Study Eligibility, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Cannabis groups: mean age 20.6 (SD 2.8) years, 68.4% male (abstract; 68.1% in the Results), mean age at first use 15.2 (SD 1.5). Comparison groups: mean age 20.8 (SD 3.4), 55.8% male. Studies mainly from the United States, United Kingdom, Europe and Australia, published 1973 to 2017 (Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph). Age ranges in the Table run from 10-23 to 18-50.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the included studies.
sample.selection_effects: English-language, peer-reviewed literature only, without grey literature. Most groups were small, most included studies enrolled people who used frequently or had a cannabis use disorder (Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 3rd paragraph), and one study by the review's first author (Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort: 227 people who used cannabis, 3,401 comparison participants, no abstinence required) supplies 52% of the comparison participants (editors' arithmetic). By their titles, at least 18 of the 62 publications were designed around another drug or a disorder (ecstasy or polydrug use 9, inhalant use 4, schizophrenia 3, ADHD 1, ketamine and cocaine dependence 1); which subgroups entered the analysis is in the supplement (not read). Excluding studies with participants with psychosis (16) and studies reporting only IQ (3) shapes what the pool can say.

exposure.measurement: As defined by each included study: frequent, heavy or problematic use, most included studies enrolling people who used frequently or had a cannabis use disorder; how use was measured and defined is tabulated only in the supplement. The authors call heterogeneity in measuring cannabis use a substantial limitation of this literature (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable: studies measured use over different periods (past year, past month), frequency units (per week, per day) and quantities (grams, joints), and cannabinoid content was not characterized; the only exposure moderators tested were age at first use (study means; early versus late onset defined between 15 and 18 by each study) and required or reported abstinence.
exposure.polysubstance: Not adjusted: effect sizes came primarily from raw scores, so they do not account for other substance use (Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 4th paragraph). Whether studies matched groups on alcohol use was tested as a moderator, with no significant difference (Results › Follow-up Analyses, 2nd paragraph). Several included studies came from research on ecstasy or polydrug use, inhalant use or combined alcohol and cannabis use (by their titles).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Required abstinence before testing varied from none to 2,160 hours (mean 152.7 hours, SD 335.2): 22 studies (32%) required none or did not say, 32 (46%) required 1 to 72 hours, 15 (22%) more than 72 hours; only 14 studies reported monitored abstinence (Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph). So in up to a third of studies participants may have been tested soon after use.

comparison.controls: Comparison participants with minimal cannabis use, as each study defined it (n=6,575 as reported).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; matching varied by study. Whether studies matched groups on alcohol use was examined as a moderator.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use cognitive baseline in any pooled comparison (cross-sectional data only); premorbid IQ, attention or conduct problems, socioeconomic status and psychiatric comorbidity are not accounted for in raw-score effect sizes. The authors note that adolescents at risk of substance use problems may show cognitive vulnerabilities before use (Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 5th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported in the main text; comparison groups' alcohol, tobacco and other drug use varied by study (details in the supplement, not read).

outcomes.instruments: Standardized neurocognitive tests from each study, assigned by construct validity to 10 domains: attention, learning, delayed memory, speed of information processing, verbal/language, visuospatial, motor, and three executive-function subdomains (abstraction/shifting, updating/working memory, inhibition); tests by domain are in the supplement (Methods › Data Extraction).
outcomes.validity_norms: Effect sizes were computed primarily from raw scores; some included studies used demographically adjusted normative data (Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 4th paragraph). No appraisal of test quality or of the included studies.
outcomes.operationalization: Hedges-corrected standardized mean difference d per test, inverse-variance weighted, signed so that negative values mean worse performance in the cannabis group; measures selected for construct validity rather than significance, avoiding several indices from one test (Methods › Effect Size Calculation; Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. 11 counts the overall estimate and the 10 domain estimates; differences between domains were tested with Bonferroni correction, but the moderator tests (treatment seeking P = .04; mean hours of abstinence P = .04) are uncorrected, and the abstinence subgroup test (P = .01) is one of several predetermined moderator analyses; the authors say the abstinence associations hold at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons (Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Searches, screening and extraction were each done independently by two researchers, with a third resolving extraction discrepancies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Overall d -0.247 (SE 0.038; 95% CI -0.32 to -0.17), between-study variance 0.070 (SE 0.018; P < .001); no I-squared or prediction interval reported. Editors' calculation (normal random effects, d plus or minus 1.96 times the square root of the variance plus SE squared): approximate 95% prediction interval -0.77 to +0.28. Domains: learning -0.33 (-0.42 to -0.24); executive abstraction/shifting -0.30 (-0.40 to -0.20); speed of processing -0.26 (-0.38 to -0.15); delayed memory -0.26 (-0.35 to -0.16); executive inhibition -0.25 (-0.38 to -0.13); executive updating/working memory -0.22 (-0.31 to -0.12); attention -0.21 (-0.31 to -0.12); verbal/language -0.14 (-0.27 to 0.001; P = .05); visuospatial -0.04 (-0.16 to 0.08); motor -0.02 (-0.22 to 0.18); domains differ overall (chi-square 41.14, 9 df, P < .001), but learning, delayed memory, attention, speed and executive domains do not differ after Bonferroni correction. Abstinence: required more than 72 hours (k = 15; n = 928) d -0.08 (-0.22 to 0.07; P = .29) vs 72 hours or less (k = 54; n = 7,799) d -0.30 (-0.37 to -0.22), difference chi-square 6.36, P = .01; mean reported hours of abstinence (k = 28; n = 1,661) beta 0.059, P = .04 uncorrected. Treatment-seeking samples (k = 12; n = 581) d -0.43 (-0.62 to -0.24) vs others (k = 56; n = 8,146) -0.22 (-0.29 to -0.14), chi-square 4.32, uncorrected P = .04. No significant moderation by sample age group, early vs late onset, alcohol matching or publication period; mean age, mean age at first use and the group difference in depression not associated. Small-study effects: Egger t = 4.70, P < .001; trim-and-fill (univariate random effects, 44 effect sizes filled) d -0.206 (-0.24 to -0.16) to -0.128 (-0.17 to -0.09), about 37.9% smaller.
analysis.covariates: None at effect-size level (raw-score differences). Study-level moderators: sample age category, mean age, age at first use (mean, early vs late), sociodemographic and clinical characteristics (group difference in depression), publication year, mean reported abstinence hours, required abstinence over 72 hours, treatment seeking, alcohol matching (Results › Follow-up Analyses, 1st paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the inclusion criteria are described as defined a priori and the moderators as predetermined (Methods › Study Eligibility, 1st paragraph; Results › Follow-up Analyses, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Domain-level numbers of studies and effect sizes, domain heterogeneity and the moderator estimates for age, onset and alcohol matching are only in the supplement (eResults, eFigures 2 and 3). The 72-hours-or-less estimate (-0.30) appears only in the abstract; the separate estimates for 0-hour and 1-to-72-hour studies appear only as points in Figure 3 (its axis was not legible in the rendering; values not extracted).
analysis.power: Not addressed. Moderator analyses are study-level comparisons; the more-than-72-hours subgroup has 15 studies (n = 928), whose interval (-0.22 to 0.07) includes no difference and reaches -0.22, close to the overall estimate of -0.25.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 69 mostly small cross-sectional samples (2,152 people who used cannabis frequently, 6,575 comparison participants, mean age about 21), cannabis groups scored on average a quarter of a standard deviation lower (d -0.25, -0.32 to -0.17), with substantial between-study spread (editors' approximate prediction interval -0.77 to +0.28) and significant small-study effects (trim-and-fill estimate about -0.13). Differences were similar across learning, memory, attention, speed and executive domains (-0.21 to -0.33) and absent for visuospatial and motor tests. Studies that required more than 72 hours of abstinence found a smaller difference (d -0.08, -0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies) than the others (-0.30), and treatment-seeking samples a larger one (-0.43); no moderation by age or age at first use was detected.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the associations are small and may be of questionable clinical importance for most individuals, that "abstinence of longer than 72 hours diminishes cognitive deficits associated with cannabis use", and that earlier studies may have overstated the magnitude and persistence of deficits; the Key Points say deficits are substantially diminished with abstinence, and the Conclusions speak of restored cognitive functioning. Gaps: (1) the abstinence result compares different studies, not the same people before and after stopping, so it cannot show that deficits diminish or are restored; studies requiring longer abstinence also differ in other ways (7 of the 15 come from papers that list the same author, S. F. Tapert, and 11 have age ranges ending at 20 or younger), and two of the 15 rows apparently share their comparison group with a row in the other subgroup; (2) the more-than-72-hours interval (-0.22 to 0.07) includes no difference but reaches -0.22, close to the overall estimate of -0.25, so it does not show that no deficit remains; (3) small and of questionable clinical importance is a statement about the mean, while the spread between studies is wide and treatment-seeking samples showed d -0.43; (4) no difference by age is a non-significant comparison between study means among samples whose mean age is 26 or less, so adolescents are compared with young adults, not with adults generally; (5) all estimates are unadjusted raw-score differences without pre-use baselines; the authors expect adjustment for confounders to shrink them, and differences that predate use would also mean the pooled values overstate any effect of cannabis. Against this, the Discussion disclaims causal inference, reports and discusses small-study bias, and notes that its abstinence finding contrasts with the Dunedin cohort and with another systematic review.

timeline.event: Grant et al. (ref. 52), the oldest included study; included studies span 1973 to 2017.
Pope et al. (ref. 101), monitored abstinence in people with long-term use: cited for deficits that diminish when abstinence is carefully monitored.

Grant et al. (ref. 23) and Schreiner and Dunn (2012, ref. 24), meta-analyses in adults: small effects, almost undetectable after a few days to weeks of abstinence; this review calls its own findings consistent with them.

The first author's meta-analysis of methamphetamine and cognition (ref. 35), cited with other drug meta-analyses as showing medium to large effects, the authors' argument that the tests are sensitive enough.

Meier et al. (ref. 102), Dunedin cohort: called the strongest evidence of dysfunction after adolescent-onset persistent heavy use, with the caveat that the subgroup was small; the abstinence finding is said to contrast with it.

Rogeberg (ref. 116) and Daly (ref. 115), letters arguing that socioeconomic status and personality may confound the Dunedin association, cited for the point that confounders are common in case-control studies of cannabis.
Ganzer et al. (ref. 25), systematic review of long-term effects in abstinent adolescents and adults, whose conclusions on persistence this review says it contradicts.

Jackson et al. (ref. 121), two longitudinal twin studies, cited with Meier et al. (2018, ref. 118, co-twin control) as large studies questioning cannabis as a cause of cognitive change once confounders and familial factors are accounted for.
Systematic review of 2004-2015 task-based studies in the project's Tier A list, not cited by this review.
Narrative review in the project's Tier A list, not cited by this review.
National Academies report (ref. 91), with which the authors say their findings converge: substantial uncertainty about deficits after sustained abstinence.
Scott et al. (ref. 16), the authors' own Philadelphia Neurodevelopmental Cohort analysis, the largest included sample (227 vs 3,401; no abstinence required).
Later tests in the project's lists, not appraised here: co-twin control analyses of cognitive functioning (Schaefer et al., 2022) and the Dunedin follow-up at 45 (Meier et al., 2022).

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of cognition restricted to young samples in the project's list; its headline is that cognitive differences in young people who use cannabis are small and fade with abstinence. The pooled differences are unadjusted cross-sectional associations of about a quarter of a standard deviation, possibly inflated by small-study effects; the abstinence result is a between-study association. Its conclusions on persistence rest on the same kind of evidence as the adult meta-analyses it cites, and on longitudinal and co-twin studies it discusses but did not pool (Meier et al., 2012, 2018; Jackson et al., 2016). Claims should cite it for the size and spread of cross-sectional differences by domain and for the study-level association with required abstinence, naming those limits; claims about recovery in people who stop need within-person studies.

Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that test cognition before first use and repeatedly afterwards, with biologically verified periods of abstinence, retested comparison groups to account for practice effects, and sibling or twin comparisons or adjustment for premorbid ability and other drug use, pooled as individual participant data; a within-person study of people who stop after frequent use, against people who continue and people who do not use, would test recovery directly.

domains.note: Population (sample mean age 26 or younger), exposure (heavy, frequent or problematic use), comparator (appropriate comparison group with minimal use) and outcome (standardized neurocognitive tests) stated (Methods › Study Eligibility, 1st paragraph).
No protocol or registration is mentioned; only a priori inclusion criteria and predetermined moderators are described.
Only cross-sectional data, with the reason (too few, heterogeneous longitudinal studies) and baseline data taken from longitudinal studies (Methods › Study Eligibility, 2nd paragraph).

Four databases searched independently by two authors, an example PubMed strategy in the supplement (not read) and bibliographies of four qualitative reviews; but limited to English-language, peer-reviewed studies without a stated reason, with no grey literature, registries or experts consulted for further studies. Under item 4 as written (senior decision 21, 25 October 2026) an unexplained language or publication-type limit is judged no.
All identified articles reviewed independently by the same two authors (Methods › Search Strategies and Study Selection).
Independent extraction by two researchers, discrepancies resolved by a third (Methods › Data Extraction).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 counts full-text exclusions by reason (291 printed; the reasons sum to 289), but no list of excluded studies appears in the article, and none is among the supplement's listed contents (eMethods, eResults, eTables 1 and 2, eFigures 1 to 3; the supplement itself was not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: The Table gives each sample's group sizes, domains tested, age range and required abstinence; exposure definitions, comparison-group characteristics, sex and setting are only in the supplement.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality assessment of the included studies is reported; study features (abstinence, treatment seeking, alcohol matching) were examined only as moderators.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: The two-level multivariate model appropriately handles several effect sizes per study, with Hedges correction and inverse-variance weights. But the pooled values are unadjusted raw-score differences from non-randomized studies, pooled without a stated justification (the lack of adjustment is acknowledged only as a limitation), and rows that share a comparison group (seven publications with two rows each) enter the model as separate studies. A close call, since adjusted estimates are rarely reported in this literature.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Risk of bias was not assessed, so its impact was not analysed; the alcohol-matching moderator is the nearest analysis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion says the effects may be overestimates (small-study effects), that raw scores do not account for sociodemographic, psychiatric or substance-use confounders, that pre-existing deficits are not accounted for and that no causal conclusion can be drawn (Considerations for Interpretation, 4th and 5th paragraphs). The abstinence conclusions do not carry these caveats (see interpretation_gap).
Between-study variance reported and tested (0.070, P < .001) and explored with predetermined moderators; I-squared and prediction intervals are not reported.

Funnel plot, Egger test (t = 4.70, P < .001) and trim-and-fill, with their implications discussed (Results › Preliminary Analyses, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 4th paragraph).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items fail (2, no protocol; 4, English-language and peer-reviewed limits without a reason; 7, no list of excluded studies; 9, no appraisal of the included studies; 11, unadjusted raw-score differences pooled without justification), so confidence is critically low under AMSTAR 2. This judges how far the pooled d can be trusted as an unbiased summary, not the review's usefulness: it models several outcomes per study properly, tests and discusses small-study effects, and states that it cannot address causation. In practice, the overall d of -0.25 is an unadjusted cross-sectional difference that small-study effects may inflate (trim-and-fill about -0.13), with wide spread between studies; the abstinence contrast is a comparison between studies, with about half of the more-than-72-hours group from studies by one research group, and cannot show recovery within people. Cite it for the size and spread of cross-sectional differences by domain and for the study-level association with required abstinence, with these caveats.

key_findings.finding: Flow: 2,562 records from databases and 30 from other sources; 1,324 after duplicates; 961 excluded on title and abstract; 363 full texts assessed; 74 articles met the criteria; 5 removed for overlapping samples, leaving 69 studies. Searches ran 10 December 2016 to 12 May 2017 in PubMed, PsycINFO, Academic Search Premier and Scopus, limited to English-language peer-reviewed studies, run and screened independently by two authors.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search Strategies and Study Selection, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Data Sources; Figure 1 (printed counts, read from the rendered image)

key_findings.finding: Full-text exclusions by reason: 67 no relevant neurocognitive testing, 48 no cannabis-only group, 35 outside the age range, 34 no appropriate comparison group, 29 measures only during neuroimaging, 19 reviews, 17 insufficient data, 16 participants with psychosis, 8 acute use, 7 prenatal exposure, 5 insufficient cannabis data, 3 IQ measures only, 1 intervention study.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (printed counts, read from the rendered image)
key_findings.note: The reasons sum to 289, while the box total reads 291 (see reporting issues). Studies reporting only IQ were excluded, as were longitudinal follow-ups (Methods › Study Eligibility, 2nd paragraph), so IQ cohorts such as Dunedin are outside the pool.

key_findings.finding: 69 studies with 8,727 participants: 2,152 in cannabis groups (mean age 20.6, SD 2.8; 68.1% male in the Results, 1,472 or 68.4% in the abstract; mean age at first use 15.2, SD 1.5) and 6,575 comparison participants with minimal cannabis use (mean age 20.8, SD 3.4; 55.8% male); 384 effect sizes; published 1973 to 2017. Required abstinence averaged 152.7 hours (SD 335.2): 22 studies (32%) none or unspecified, 32 (46%) 1 to 72 hours, 15 (22%) more than 72 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results; Table
key_findings.note: The Table's 69 rows come from 62 publications, and its columns sum to 2,188 and 6,573 participants (editors' arithmetic); the authors' own Philadelphia cohort study supplies 227 of the cannabis and 3,401 of the comparison participants.

key_findings.finding: Overall difference in neurocognitive performance, cannabis groups vs comparison groups (raw-score standardized mean differences, multivariate mixed-effects model): d -0.247 (SE 0.038; 95% CI -0.32 to -0.17); between-study variance 0.070 (SE 0.018; P < .001), more than sampling error alone.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: approximate 95% prediction interval -0.77 to +0.28 (normal random effects, treating the reported variance as the variance of study means).

key_findings.finding: Small-study effects: the funnel plot was asymmetric and Egger's test significant (t = 4.70, P < .001); Duval and Tweedie trim-and-fill (univariate random effects, since no multivariate method exists) filled 44 effect sizes and reduced d from -0.206 (-0.24 to -0.16) to -0.128 (-0.17 to -0.09), about 37.9%, still significant; the authors advise caution about the exact reduction and say the effects may be overestimates.
key_findings.locator: Results › Preliminary Analyses, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: By domain (d, 95% CI): learning -0.33 (-0.42 to -0.24); executive abstraction/shifting -0.30 (-0.40 to -0.20); speed of information processing -0.26 (-0.38 to -0.15); delayed memory -0.26 (-0.35 to -0.16); executive inhibition -0.25 (-0.38 to -0.13); executive updating/working memory -0.22 (-0.31 to -0.12); attention -0.21 (-0.31 to -0.12); verbal/language -0.14 (-0.27 to 0.001; P = .05); visuospatial -0.04 (-0.16 to 0.08; P = .53); motor -0.02 (-0.22 to 0.18; P = .83). Domains differed overall (chi-square 41.14, 9 df, P < .001), but learning, delayed memory, attention, speed and executive domains did not differ from one another after Bonferroni correction.
key_findings.note: Numbers of studies and effect sizes per domain are only in the supplement (eResults, not read); Figure 2 is an image.

key_findings.finding: No significant differences in effect size by sample age category (adolescents vs adults), early vs late onset (cut-offs between 15 and 18, as each study defined), alcohol matching or period of publication; mean age, mean age at first use and the group difference in depression were not associated with effect size. Treatment-seeking samples (k = 12; n = 581) showed a larger difference, d -0.43 (-0.62 to -0.24), than others (k = 56; n = 8,146), d -0.22 (-0.29 to -0.14); chi-square 4.32, uncorrected P = .04.
key_findings.note: Study-level (ecological) comparisons; the age comparison is between samples with mean ages of 26 or less. Estimates for age, onset and alcohol matching are only in the supplement.

key_findings.finding: Abstinence: longer mean reported abstinence (k = 28; n = 1,661) went with smaller differences (beta 0.059; P = .04, uncorrected). Studies requiring more than 72 hours of abstinence (k = 15; n = 928) had d -0.08 (95% CI -0.22 to 0.07; P = .29), smaller than studies requiring 72 hours or less (k = 54; n = 7,799; d -0.30, -0.37 to -0.22); chi-square 6.36, P = .01. Figure 3 also plots studies requiring no abstinence (k = 22) and 1 to 72 hours (k = 32) separately, to show that the unknown or zero-abstinence studies do not drive the difference.
key_findings.locator: Results › Follow-up Analyses, 3rd paragraph; Abstract › Results; Figure 3 legend
key_findings.note: A between-study comparison, not a within-person change. The more-than-72-hours interval includes no difference and reaches -0.22, close to the overall estimate of -0.25, which lies just outside it, so it does not exclude a difference of nearly the overall size. The -0.30 estimate for the other 54 studies is printed only in the Abstract. The authors describe the abstinence associations as holding at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons (Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph). Figure 3 values were not extracted (axis not legible in the rendering). The unit of the beta for abstinence hours is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Composition of the more-than-72-hours subgroup (editors' reading of the Table and reference list): its 15 rows require 168 to 2,160 hours; 7 come from papers that list S. F. Tapert among their authors (refs 11, 54, 55, 61, 67, 78, 90) and an eighth (ref. 62) shares its first two authors with one of them; 11 have age ranges ending at 20 or younger; Fried et al. (2005) and Schweinsburg et al. (2010) each contribute one row to each abstinence subgroup, with a comparison group of the same size in both rows (apparently shared). The Table's rows for this subgroup sum to 947 participants against the reported 928.
key_findings.locator: Table (Minimum Required Abstinence Period column); reference list
key_findings.note: Editors' observation, not the authors'; it means the abstinence contrast may also reflect laboratory, sample and protocol differences.

key_findings.finding: The authors describe the association between length of abstinence and effect sizes as holding at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons. Only 14 studies reported monitored abstinence. The authors read the abstinence result as suggesting that some deficits reflect residual effects of recent use or withdrawal rather than persistent change, and note that it contrasts with a large longitudinal study (Dunedin) and with a recent systematic review of abstinent adolescents and adults (Ganzer et al., 2016).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors state that effect sizes were computed mainly from raw scores and so do not account for sociodemographic, psychiatric or substance-use confounders; that results do not account for deficits that may have existed before use, so no causal conclusion can be drawn; that most included studies enrolled people who used frequently or had a cannabis use disorder, so findings may not apply to occasional use or to medical cannabinoids; and that longitudinal evidence conflicts, citing Dunedin as strong evidence for adolescent-onset persistent heavy use (small subgroup) and two large studies, including a co-twin study, that question a causal role.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Considerations for Interpretation, 3rd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: All domain effect sizes were below one-third of a standard deviation, which the authors take to argue against medium or large deficits, citing medium to large effects in meta-analyses of alcohol, methamphetamine, benzodiazepines and cocaine as evidence that the tests are sensitive.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Findings Across Cognitive Domains, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The statement holds for the domain estimates but not for the treatment-seeking subgroup (d -0.43); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: statistically significant but small associations; little evidence of more severe effects with use at earlier ages or in adolescence; longer abstinence associated with smaller group differences and with what the authors call restored cognitive functioning; very small, non-significant differences in studies requiring more than 72 hours of abstinence; large longitudinal studies needed.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance; Key Points › Meaning

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the cannabis groups as 1,472 (68.4%) male, which matches 1,472 of 2,152; the Results give 68.1% male.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Results report 384 effect sizes from 69 studies with a mean (SD) of 9.46 (5.32) per study, range 1 to 17; 384 divided by 69 is 5.6 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Preliminary Analyses, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the count of effect sizes or the mean per study is wrong, or the mean describes something else; the number of effect sizes behind the estimates cannot be checked from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: In Figure 1 the box for excluded full texts reads 291, but its 13 reasons sum to 289; 363 minus 289 gives the 74 articles that met the criteria.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor arithmetic error in the flowchart; the flow is otherwise consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 derives 69 studies from 74 articles minus 5 with overlapping samples, but the Table's 69 rows cite 62 distinct publications: Cousijn 2013, Ehrenreich 1999, Filbey 2015, Fried 2005, Gruber 2012, Schweinsburg 2010 and Tait 2011 each contribute two rows with the same comparison-group size, and the two Tait rows are identical in every column.
reporting_issues.consequence: The unit called a study is a sample; rows sharing a comparison group enter the model as independent studies, count their comparison participants twice in the totals, and in two cases fall in opposite abstinence subgroups, so the subgroup test is not between independent sets.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table's group sizes sum to 2,188 in cannabis groups and 6,573 in comparison groups (8,761 in all), against the reported 2,152, 6,575 and 8,727; its rows for studies requiring more than 72 hours sum to 947 and the rest to 7,814, against the reported 928 and 7,799 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table; Results › Follow-up Analyses, 3rd paragraph; Abstract › Results
reporting_issues.consequence: The participant counts cannot be reproduced from the Table; quote them as reported, with the caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The treatment-seeking comparison counts 12 plus 56 = 68 studies, one short of 69, although its participant counts (581 plus 8,146) add up to the full 8,727.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Follow-up Analyses, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: One study is unaccounted for in the study counts; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says all effect sizes in the study were below one-third of a standard deviation, while the Results report d -0.43 for treatment-seeking samples.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Findings Across Cognitive Domains, 1st paragraph; Results › Follow-up Analyses, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The small-effects statement applies to the overall and domain means, not to every subgroup; claims about people in treatment should use the subgroup estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The text cites eTable 1 for the tests in each domain and eTable 2 for the fuller per-study overview and the cannabis-use measures, while the supplement's listed contents name eTable 1 as the overview of the 69 studies and eTable 2 as the tests by domain.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data Extraction; Table footnote; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph; Supplementary Materials list
reporting_issues.consequence: Cross-references to the supplement are swapped; a reader of the supplement must look in the other table.

reporting_issues.issue: Ganzer et al. (2016, ref. 25) is counted in the Introduction as one of three meta-analyses of adults and described in the Discussion as a systematic review of adolescents and adults, while the Introduction also states that no meta-analysis of adolescents or young adults existed.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Introduction, 4th paragraph; Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Overlap with earlier syntheses is described inconsistently; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The trim-and-fill starting value (d -0.206, -0.24 to -0.16) comes from a univariate random-effects model applied to the effect sizes, not from the main multivariate estimate (-0.247, -0.32 to -0.17), and its narrower interval suggests the 384 effect sizes were treated as independent; the Egger test probably likewise.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Preliminary Analyses, 3rd and 4th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted estimate of -0.128 and the Egger P value are approximate, as the authors caution; the direction (inflation by small studies) is the usable result.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6137521 (JAMA Psychiatry 2018;75(6):585-595), read in the app's browser on 2026-10-27: all sections, Key Points, the Table (69 rows, rendered as text and summed by the editors), the legends of Figures 1 to 3, the counts printed in the Figure 1 flowchart (read from the rendered image), article information (contributions, conflict-of-interest disclosures, funding, role of the funder, additional contributions) and the reference list. Figures 2 and 3 are images whose plotted values were not extracted (the domain values are in the text; the Figure 3 axis was not legible in the rendering). The supplement (one PDF: eMethods, eResults, eTables 1 and 2, eFigures 1 to 3) was not opened; per-study exposure definitions, domain-level numbers of studies, heterogeneity by domain and the moderator estimates for age, onset and alcohol matching depend on it.

disagreements.first_pass: A between-study comparison, not a within-person change. The more-than-72-hours interval includes the overall estimate of -0.25. Figure 3 values were not extracted (axis not legible in the rendering). The unit of the beta for abstinence hours is not stated.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 215, corrected: the numbers are right but the note is wrong; the more-than-72-hours interval (-0.22 to 0.07) does not include the overall estimate (-0.247) and overlaps the overall interval only between -0.22 and -0.17; the -0.30 estimate is printed only in the Abstract; the authors call the abstinence associations uncorrected.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after checking the saved PMC text (Abstract › Results; Results › Preliminary Analyses, 2nd paragraph; Follow-up Analyses, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Length of Abstinence, 1st paragraph): -0.247 lies below -0.22. Note rewritten with the reader's three points; the finding's numbers are unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: (2) the more-than-72-hours interval (-0.22 to 0.07) includes the overall estimate, so it does not show that no deficit remains;
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 215: the same interval error as key finding 7; the conclusion of point (2) still holds because the interval reaches -0.22.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted (same check as key finding 7); wording corrected, conclusion and gap rating unchanged.

disagreements.first_pass: ...the more-than-72-hours subgroup has 15 studies (n = 928), whose interval (-0.22 to 0.07) includes the overall estimate.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 215, missed: analysis.power repeats the interval error.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted; corrected as in key finding 7.

disagreements.first_pass: Only 14 studies reported monitored abstinence. The authors read the abstinence result as suggesting...
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 215, missed: the same paragraph says the abstinence associations hold only at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons; no key finding records the authors' own statement.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: confirmed in Discussion › Length of Abstinence and Reduction of Effect Sizes, 1st paragraph ('albeit at thresholds uncorrected for multiple comparisons'); added to key finding 9, whose locator already names that paragraph.

disagreements.first_pass: ...the abstinence subgroup test (P = .01) is one of several predetermined moderator analyses.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 215, missed (as above): claims citing P = .01 should mark it as uncorrected.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted; the authors' statement added with its place.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 215, missed (minor): the authors cite the National Academies report as concluding there is significant uncertainty about deficits after sustained abstinence; as a key finding it would support the after-stopping claim.
disagreements.resolution: Not added: confirmed in the Discussion's 1st paragraph, but it is the review's citation of another body's conclusion, already recorded in the replication timeline; a claim must not present it as this review's finding.
